suggestions.rationale: Depressive symptoms and depressive disorders are common in people with heart failure and warrant clinical assessment. This comorbidity evidence supports research of the relationship but does not by itself establish that heart failure caused or aggravated an individual depressive disorder; diagnosis, chronology, functional burden, treatment, and competing contributors require case-specific review.
evidenceGaps: Qualified diagnosis of a depressive disorder rather than symptom-screening results alone
Chronology comparing depressive-disorder onset or worsening with heart-failure onset, severity, decompensations, functional limitation, and treatment
Documentation of heart-failure functional burden and relevant treatment history
Evaluation of alternative psychiatric, medical, medication-related, psychosocial, substance-use, and sleep-related contributors
Qualified cardiovascular or mental-health opinion addressing the individual relationship if causation or aggravation is asserted

sourceReferences.citation: Depression in Heart Failure: A Systematic Review
sourceReferences.note: Clinical evidence documenting depression as a common comorbidity in heart failure; supports clinical relevance and assessment, not an automatic individual causal nexus.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The published knowledge base includes this relationship as an association: Depressive symptoms and depressive disorders are common in people with heart failure and warrant clinical assessment. This comorbidity evidence supports research of the relationship but does not by itself establish that heart failure caused or aggravated an individual depressive disorder; diagnosis, chronology, functional burden, treatment, and competing contributors require case-specific review.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation under 38 CFR § 3.310 is established by the current evidence; the guard explicitly limits the claim to association.
